section: 15.4
title: Irreducibility of Induced Representations
---

An induced representation need not be irreducible. For instance, $\Ind^G_{\{e\}} \CC = R_G$ contains every irreducible representation of $G$. Since $\Ind W$ is irreducible if and only if $\langle \chi_{\Ind W}, \chi_{\Ind W} \rangle_G = 1$, and Frobenius reciprocity gives $$\langle \chi_{\Ind W}, \chi_{\Ind W} \rangle_G = \langle \chi_W, \chi_{\Res \Ind W} \rangle_H,$$ the question comes down to understanding $\Res^G_H \Ind^G_H W$. We do this when $H$ is normal.

Let $H \trianglelefteq G$, let $W$ be a representation of $H$ given by $\rho : H \to \GL(W)$, and let $g \in G$. The ***conjugate representation*** $W^g$ is the space $W$ with $h \in H$ acting by $\rho(g^{-1} h g)$; this makes sense because $g^{-1}hg \in H$. Its character is $\chi_{W^g}(h) = \chi_W(g^{-1}hg)$. The representations $W$ and $W^g$ have the same invariant subspaces, so $W^g$ is irreducible if $W$ is. For $h_0 \in H$, the map $\rho(h_0) : W^{gh_0} \to W^g$ is an isomorphism of representations, since $\rho(h_0)\rho(h_0^{-1} g^{-1} h g h_0) = \rho(g^{-1}hg)\rho(h_0)$; so the isomorphism class of $W^g$ depends only on the coset $gH$, and $W^{h_0} \cong W$.

:::lemma{15.4.1} Restricting an induced representation to a normal subgroup
Let $H \trianglelefteq G$, let $\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_k$ be representatives of the cosets of $H$, and let $W$ be a representation of $H$. Then $$\Res^G_H \Ind^G_H W \cong W^{\sigma_1} \oplus \cdots \oplus W^{\sigma_k}.$$
:::

:::proof
Each summand $\sigma_i W$ of $\Ind W$ is $H$-invariant: for $h \in H$, we have $h\sigma_i = \sigma_i(\sigma_i^{-1} h \sigma_i)$ with $\sigma_i^{-1} h \sigma_i \in H$, so $h(\sigma_i w) = \sigma_i\bigl((\sigma_i^{-1} h \sigma_i) w\bigr)$. This says exactly that the linear isomorphism $W \to \sigma_i W$, $w \mapsto \sigma_i w$, is an isomorphism of representations of $H$ from $W^{\sigma_i}$ to $\sigma_i W$.
:::

:::proposition{15.4.2} Induction from a normal subgroup
Let $H \trianglelefteq G$ and let $W$ be an irreducible representation of $H$. Then $\langle \chi_{\Ind W}, \chi_{\Ind W} \rangle_G$ is the number of cosets $gH \in G/H$ with $W^g \cong W$. In particular, $\Ind^G_H W$ is irreducible if and only if $W^g \not\cong W$ for every $g \in G \setminus H$.
:::

:::proof
By Frobenius reciprocity and Lemma [15.4.1](/notes/math-55a/15-4-irreducibility-of-induced-representations#lemma-15-4-1), $$\langle \chi_{\Ind W}, \chi_{\Ind W} \rangle_G = \langle \chi_W, \chi_{\Res \Ind W} \rangle_H = \sum_{i=1}^k \langle \chi_W, \chi_{W^{\sigma_i}} \rangle_H.$$ Each $W^{\sigma_i}$ is irreducible, so the $i$th term is $1$ if $W^{\sigma_i} \cong W$ and $0$ otherwise. The coset $H$ itself always counts, since $W^{h} \cong W$ for $h \in H$; so the sum equals $1$ exactly when no other coset counts.
:::

:::note
For a subgroup $H$ that is not normal, Mackey’s analysis of $\Res^G_H \Ind^G_H W$ leads to the following criterion, which we state without proof (see Serre, *Linear Representations of Finite Groups*, §7.4). Let $W$ be an irreducible representation of $H$, given by $\rho$, and for $g \in G$ let $H_g = H \cap gHg^{-1}$. Then $\Ind^G_H W$ is irreducible if and only if, for every $g \in G \setminus H$, the two representations $x \mapsto \rho(x)$ and $x \mapsto \rho(g^{-1}xg)$ of $H_g$ have no irreducible constituent in common. When $H$ is normal, $H_g = H$ and this is Proposition [15.4.2](/notes/math-55a/15-4-irreducibility-of-induced-representations#proposition-15-4-2).
:::

:::example{15.4.3} Inducing from a subgroup of index 2
Let $[G:H] = 2$. Then $H$ is normal, since its two left cosets $H$ and $G \setminus H$ are also its two right cosets. Fix $g \in G \setminus H$ and an irreducible representation $W$ of $H$. By Proposition [15.4.2](/notes/math-55a/15-4-irreducibility-of-induced-representations#proposition-15-4-2):

- if $W^g \not\cong W$, then $\Ind^G_H W$ is irreducible;
- if $W^g \cong W$, then $\langle \chi_{\Ind W}, \chi_{\Ind W} \rangle_G = 2$, so $\Ind W \cong X \oplus Y$ with $X$ and $Y$ irreducible and not isomorphic.

In the second case $\dim X = \dim Y = \dim W$. Indeed, by Frobenius reciprocity $\langle \chi_W, \chi_{\Res X} \rangle_H = \langle \chi_{\Ind W}, \chi_X \rangle_G = 1$, so $\Res X$ contains $W$ and $\dim X \geq \dim W$; likewise $\dim Y \geq \dim W$; and $\dim X + \dim Y = 2 \dim W$.

For $G = S_3$ and $H = A_3$, take $g = (12)$. Since $(12)^{-1}(123)(12) = (132)$, we get $\chi_\omega^{(12)} = \chi_{\omega^2} \not\cong \chi_\omega$, so $\Ind \chi_\omega$ is irreducible, in agreement with Example [15.2.7](/notes/math-55a/15-2-induced-representations#example-15-2-7). On the other hand the trivial representation $\chi_1$ of $A_3$ is its own conjugate, and $\Ind \chi_1 = {\CC}[S_3/A_3]$ splits as $U \oplus U'$ (Exercise [15.5.2](/notes/math-55a/15-5-example-s-4-supset-s-3#exercise-15-5-2)(2)).
:::
